items.prose: A statement in a virtual round: a fund must pay $n$ redemptions in order over $k$ days. Find the smallest daily cash limit that pays them all. $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ and each redemption is at most $10^9$.
items.question: Which pattern fits?

options.text: Binary search on the limit, with a greedy check of each guess
A sliding window over the redemptions
options.why: You matched *in order* to a window. The question asks for the smallest value that works, which is a search on the answer.
BFS finds fewest moves in a graph. There is no graph here.

options.text: Try every limit from the largest redemption upwards
options.why: That is correct but slow: up to about $2 \cdot 10^{14}$ limits, each checked in $O(n)$.

feedback.correct: Binary search on the answer: problem C in disguise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for *the smallest value that works*.

explain.text: A larger limit always works if a smaller one does, so *works* is monotone in the limit. That is the shape of problem C from the virtual round.

items.prose: Your time log for a 60-minute round reads: reading 12 minutes, coding 30, debugging 18.
items.question: What share of the round went on debugging?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the debugging minutes by the whole round.

byKey.of-code: 60% is debugging over coding, $18 / 30$. Divide by the whole hour.

explain.text: $18 / 60 = 0.3$, so 30% of the hour went on debugging. That share is the first thing to cut, with hand cases before submitting.

items.prose: Under the course's rule, a problem worth 1,500 loses 6 points a minute and 50 per rejected attempt. Its floor is 30%. You solve it at minute 48 after two rejections.
items.question: What does it score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the minutes, then both rejections.

byKey.nopen: You left out both rejections, which cost 100.
byKey.onepen: You charged one rejection. There were two.

explain.text: $6 \cdot 48 = 288$ and $2 \cdot 50 = 100$, so $1500 - 388 = 1112$. That is well above the floor of 450.

items.prose: Same rule: each problem loses its value over 250 per minute until solved. P, worth 1,000, needs about 40 minutes; Q, worth 500, needs about 15.
items.question: How many more points does Q then P score than P then Q?

widget.accept: 20: $(1000 \cdot 15 - 500 \cdot 40) / 250 = -20$ for Q first, so Q first loses 20 fewer.
widget.label: Points

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the swap formula from lesson 14.

byKey.neg: −20 is the change in points lost. Losing 20 fewer means scoring 20 more.

explain.text: Q earns about 33 points a minute and P 25. Q first: P waits 15 minutes and loses 60; P first: Q waits 40 and loses 80. The difference is 20.

items.prose: A solution sums a list with `for i in range(1, len(xs)): total += xs[i]`, starting from `total = 0`. It passed the examples.
items.question: Which hand case shows the bug most directly?

options.why: That fails too, giving 4, but the single value shows the missing first element at a glance.
A large case fails without showing why. Hand cases are small on purpose.
The buggy loop also gives 0 there, so the bug stays hidden.

feedback.correct: `[5]` returns 0: the first element is never added.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest case whose answer depends on the first element.

explain.text: The loop starts at index 1, so `xs[0]` is never added. On `[5]` it returns 0 instead of 5, which points straight at the start of the range.

items.prose: In C++, problem D of lesson 16 counts the ways to cut 200,000 zeros into three equal runs: 19,999,700,001.
items.question: Which type must the count have?

options.text: `int`: it is only a count of ways
options.why: You assumed counts are small. 19,999,700,001 is far above an `int`'s 2,147,483,647.

options.text: `double`: it is a very large number
options.why: A `double` holds it exactly here, but integer counts belong in `long long`, which is exact to about $9.2 \cdot 10^{18}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the count with an `int`'s limit.

explain.text: $\binom{199999}{2} = 19{,}999{,}700{,}001$, about nine times $2^{31} - 1$. Checking types is step 3 of the debugging routine.

items.prose: Your rating is 1,350. Your last round left problems rated 1500, 1600, 1900 and 2300 unsolved.
items.question: Which do you upsolve now? Select all that apply.

options.why: 1900 is 550 above you. Note it and come back later.
2300 is 950 above you, too far for now.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep problems up to about 1,650.

explain.text: $1350 + 300 = 1650$, so 1500 and 1600 are in range. The others go in the log for later.

items.prose: Minute 95 of a two-hour round. The scoreboard shows E solved by many more than D. E is worth 1,250 and loses 5 points a minute, with 50 per rejection and a 30% floor. You expect to need 20 minutes.
items.question: What will E score if you solve it then with no rejections?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The score decays from the start of the round, not from minute 95.

byKey.twenty: You decayed it for 20 minutes only. The score falls from minute 0, so use the solve minute, 115.
byKey.floor: 375 is the floor, but $1250 - 575 = 675$ is above it.

explain.text: E is solved at minute $95 + 20 = 115$, so it loses $5 \cdot 115 = 575$ points. That leaves 675, above the floor of 375, and E beats an unlikely D.
